title: A cooking order without recursion
prompt:
Write topo(g, root). g is a dict from an item to the list of items it needs. An item that isn't a key needs nothing. Return every item reachable from root, each exactly once, in post-order: an item's parts left to right, then the item. Items not reachable from root are left out.

Use your own stack, not recursion. One test is a chain 100,000 items deep, far past the recursion limit.

A list of (item, ready) pairs and a set of items you have started. Mark an item when it pops without its note, and skip it if it is already marked.
starter:
def topo(g: dict[str, list[str]], root: str) -> list[str]:
    return [root]

tests.expr: len(topo({f"x{i}": [f"x{i - 1}", f"x{i - 1}"] for i in range(1, 41)}, "x40"))
(lambda r: (len(r), r[0], r[-1]))(topo({str(i): [str(i + 1)] for i in range(100000)}, "0"))

hints: Keep a list `stack` of `(item, ready)` pairs, starting with `[(root, False)]`, and loop `while stack:`. `stack.pop()` takes the last one.
When an item pops without its note: if it's in your `started` set, skip it. Otherwise add it, push `(item, True)`, then push its parts with `False` in reverse order, so the first part ends up on top.
When an item pops with its note, all its parts are written, so append it to the output. Use `g.get(item, [])` for an item that needs nothing.
explain: The list holds the work a recursive walk would keep on the call stack. An item is marked when it is first expanded, so a shared part is expanded once, and it is written only when it pops again with its note, after all its parts: that is post-order. Pushing the parts in reverse puts the first one on top, so they come out left to right. Nothing recurses, so the 100,000-deep chain never meets the recursion limit.
